title: Deadly delirium; Fatal heart attack caused by mysterious condition, not Taser, doc testifies
article: In the last conscious hour of his life, Ronald Perry was possessed of superhuman strength that threatened to overwhelm the handful of city cops trying to subdue him.
His heart was racing and his respiratory rate was up to four times more rapid than normal for a man his age.
That was among the evidence heard yesterday at the opening day of a fatality inquiry into the death of the 28\-year\-old city man.
Perry died at Royal Alexandra Hospital on March 23, 2004, four days after cops zapped him multiple times with a Taser in attempts to bring him under control.
Medical examiner Dr. Bernie Bannach told the inquiry that Perry died from the effects of a massive heart attack brought on by a mysterious condition called excited delirium.
The condition can be caused by psychiatric problems, toxicity from substances such as cocaine, or chronic alcohol abuse, said Bannach.
Sufferers of excited delirium often display bizarre, aggressive, paranoid behaviour combined with almost superhuman strength.
Bannach said the Taser zaps did not play a role in Perry's death.
"The indications are that Taser electricity does not proceed into the deep tissues of the body and therefore does not affect the heart," he said.
Bannach said people who are zapped with a stun gun while they're in a state of excited delirium may die, but they die due to excited delirium, not from the electricity.
"In excited delirium (cases), the Taser is sort of a red herring," he said outside the courtroom.
Bannach said it's not exactly known how excited delirium leads to cardiac arrest, though there are some theories.
On March 19, 2004, city cops were called to the intersection of 129 Avenue and 64 Street for a report of a man running amok.
Const. Kathy Rolfe said she found Perry sitting on the hood of a Dodge Spirit, trying to pry off the antenna.
Perry was zapped twice with a stun gun as he struggled with cops at the scene.
Homicide Det. Bill Clark, who investigated the fatality, said officers at the scene told him Perry was fighting police with "superhuman strength."
Perry was zapped with a Taser several more times as he continued to struggle at Royal Alexandra Hospital, where he was transported by ambulance.
The inquiry heard that as Perry was being restrained at the hospital, he was given the drugs Haldol and Ativan.
Seconds later, he suddenly stopped breathing and went into cardiac arrest.
Medical staff managed to get his heart started again, but Perry never regained consciousness and died four days later.
Perry's family is not represented at the hearing, which continues today.
Inquiry counsel Lionel Whittaker said the family was offered the opportunity to have representation.
